summary.text:
Maldon District Council's Treasury Management Outturn 2025/26 to Strategy and Resources Committee on 23 July 2026 — a 5-page covering paper. The report is genuinely to the point but the appendix does most of the work: every prudential indicator and the CFR sit in APPENDIX 1 (Link Group economic context PLUS compliance with prudential indicators), which is referenced twice in the covering paper but is NOT in the PDF held on disk. What the covering paper DOES print is the investment position, the average yields, budgeted vs actual investment income, the outlook narrative (from MUFG, dated 22 December 2025) and the £8.552m under-borrowing figure.

Maldon is a small non-metropolitan district (population ~66k) and a net investor with essentially no external debt — a five-year hire purchase agreement on two tractors (April 2023) is the only external debt disclosed at §3.3.1. It holds zero PWLB. Our price_book agrees exactly: no borrower matching Maldon.

Investment side: £16.4m at 31/3/26 (down £3m in year), average balance £22.5m, all-portfolio yield 4.6%. Budget beat of £0.383m — actual investment income £1.047m against a £0.664m budget, 57.7% above. £5m in pooled and property funds (£3m CCLA LA Property Fund, £2m Ninety-One Diversified Income Fund) held at £4,532k fair value at 31/3/26 — an ~£468k unrealised capital loss (~9.4%), deferred under FVPL to the Financial Instruments Adjustment Account (statutory override). Internal cross-check: 4.6% × £22.5m average = £1.035m estimated income, ties to actual £1.047m within £12k.

Debt side: £8.552m of internal borrowing funding the cost of waste collection vehicles and Blackwater Leisure Centre investment, with the intention to externalise 'when necessary'. That is the only quantified balance-sheet number on the treasury side in the whole covering paper. Loan-book reconciliation ties trivially (empty on empty) and the balance-sheet identity cannot be closed because CFR is absent from both the covering paper and the pre-audit accounts covering paper (42314) — both leave that number in the appendix on the council website.

The outlook section (§3.7–§3.10) carries a MUFG Corporate Markets forecast dated 22 December 2025 into a report published for a 23 July 2026 committee — a seven-month gap between forecast and paper. Central call is 'extended interest rate pause is more likely than interest rate hikes' and 'first Bank Rate reduction in the new forecast is set at Q3 2027'. Dated and falsifiable in the sense EMAIL_TEMPLATE.md prizes, but stating a live counterpart against the OIS curve at draft-send time would need a rate snapshot beyond this repo.

Email drafted around three points: the loan-file reconciliation as a proof-of-read (zero PWLB on both sides, so worth one sentence), the £8.552m internal-borrowing decision as a live future data point we would price, and the MUFG December forecast now seven months into a market that has moved. No advice. Courses chosen to match a debt-free/nearly-debt-free district holding pooled funds under the IFRS 9 override. S151 contact on record from the paper: Ben Jay, Director of Finance — title verbatim from p.5 'Enquiries to' line; the paper does not explicitly say he is the s151 (§3.6.2 refers to 'the Section 151 Officer' in the third person as is drafting convention) but he is the report's author and the Director of Finance, so almost certainly is. No email address published in either paper on disk; recipient line will be blocked until an address is added.

officer.body:
Dear Ben,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a couple of thoughts on the Treasury Management Outturn taken to Strategy and Resources on 23 July. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Five pages for a district's annual outturn is unusual, and the report reads without noise. Our own PWLB file agrees with paragraph 3.3.1 exactly: no borrowing recorded against Maldon, matching what you print — a small check but the reason to run it is that a mis-spelled borrower name silently returns 'no debt' too, and we would rather rule that out than rely on it.

The line that stood out is the MUFG summary at paragraph 3.7. That forecast is dated 22 December 2025 and by the time it reached committee on 23 July it was seven months old. The central call — an 'extended interest rate pause' and the first Bank Rate cut set at Q3 2027 — is the kind of dated view we watch drift through the papers we read: markets have priced and re-priced that path several times over the intervening months. We publish PWLB rates at both fixings on the front of pwlbtoday.org, and the SONIA path shows what the market is pricing for Bank Rate at any given horizon — the point being that between adviser updates you can see where consensus has moved to without waiting for the next quarterly note.

The other paragraph worth mentioning is 3.3.1 — the £8.552m of internal borrowing carrying the waste collection vehicle and Blackwater Leisure Centre spend, with 'the expectation of externalising that borrowing when necessary'. Whenever that decision comes up, we price every PWLB maturity daily at both fixings and hold the full record of what the sector has drawn since April this year, so the peer-borrowing view at the moment of decision is live rather than backward-looking. The loan-analysis page at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis is where the sector's book sits; break costs there are indicative only and only the DMO can quote.

One standing point because CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates will put it in front of every S151: the liability benchmark pathway becomes central to how the whole treasury strategy is framed. Interactive version of it, tied to our rate feeds, is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity — even for a council with no external borrowing the pathway is the way to show when internal borrowing needs to convert.

On training, three fit the paper. Investment strategy for debt-free (and nearly-debt-free) councils is the closest match to Maldon's position. Cost of carry & internal borrowing decisions is the one that sits behind the timing question on the £8.552m. IFRS 9 statutory override — the 2029 cliff is worth flagging given the FVPL treatment at paragraph 3.4.3 and the extension the override has already been through. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if any of it is useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew

Source: Treasury Management Outturn 2025/26, Strategy and Resources Committee 23 July 2026, at https://democracy.maldon.gov.uk/documents/s42401/treasury-management-outturn-2025-2026.pdf.
